newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia reforms threatened by row over senator.
newsitem.headline: Australia reforms threatened by row over senator.

text.p: Australian government plans for further economic reform have come under threat as political opponents take aim at an independent senator whose vote is crucial for new legislation.

"This is really above all now a problem for the government," deputy opposition leader Gareth Evans told reporters on Thursday as Prime Minister John Howard's conservative administration faced allegations of fraud against Labor defector Mal Colston.
"They're the ones who are relying on Senator Colston's vote every inch of the way for their legislative programme," he said.
Colston quit Labor in August when the government delivered him the job of deputy president of the Senate, the upper house of parliament.
Since then Colston has usually voted for Howard's reform legislation, notably the big deficit-slashing budget.

The government is two votes short of a Senate majority and without the vote of Colston and another co-operative independent, Brian Harradine, the conservatives would get very little contentious legislation through the upper house.
All other non-government senators belong to leftist parties and the independents' support will be needed again if the government renews its budget attack this year, as it promises.
A former staff member this week accused Colston in an administrative tribunal of misusing expense allowances and of giving office jobs to relatives who did not actually work.
Colston would have to quit parliament if convicted of fraud.
Labor this week has flung more such accusations against him in parliament and government sources confirm that the police are assessing some of the claims.
Colston denies the allegations and fellow independent Harradine said on Thursday they were motivated by the Labor Party's legendary hatred of traitors.
"Would the Labor Party be doing this if Senator Colston was still a member of the Labor Party?" Harradine said. "I'm sure there's a lot of politics in it and I think it's grubby."

Administrative Services Minister David Jull, responsible for politicians' entitlements, told parliament his department had been unable so far to confirm the allegations and would have to investigate further.
